title: How a simple AI newsletter workflow saved me hours and added extra income
excerpt: I turned a weekly newsletter into a low-maintenance side hustle using AI. The workflow takes under an hour a week, frees up my schedule, and adds a steady extra income.
metaDescription: Learn the exact AI tools and steps I used to automate newsletter curation, save several hours each week, and earn extra money. Practical guide for freelancers a
author: Ali Hamza

body:
## The problem I faced
I run a freelance copywriting business and a small personal blog. Every Thursday I promised my readers a curated list of useful articles, tools, and tips. The promise felt good, but the prep ate up two to three hours each week. I spent time scanning RSS feeds, copying links, writing blurbs, and formatting the email. By the time I hit send, the time spent was almost as much as the revenue the newsletter generated, barely covering my email service fee.

I kept asking myself: Is there a way to keep the newsletter useful without the endless manual grind? If I could shave off a few hours, I could either take on more client work or turn the saved time into a small side income.

## The AI tools I tried
I tested three tools that promised to automate parts of the curation process. I kept the selection narrow on purpose - the goal was to avoid a tech stack that required constant tinkering.

**1. Feedly AI (formerly Leo)**
- Learns my reading preferences over time.
- Highlights high-engagement articles in my feeds.
- Offers a one-click “Summarize” button.

**2. Copy.ai’s “Content Refiner**
- Takes a raw paragraph and rewrites it in a concise, newsletter-ready tone.
- Provides a short list of bullet-point alternatives.

**3. MailerLite’s automation API**
- Lets me push a JSON payload directly into a draft email.
- Handles list segmentation and scheduling without manual clicks.

I avoided more exotic options like custom GPT-4 scripts because I wanted something that could be set up in a single afternoon and left alone afterward.

## Putting the pieces together
The workflow I landed on has four clear steps. Each step can be done on a laptop or even a phone, and the whole thing fits into a 45-minute window on a typical Thursday.

**Step 1 - Capture the raw feed**
- I let Feedly AI scan three niche newsletters and two industry blogs I already follow.
- At 9 am I open the “Highlights” tab and click “Export to CSV”. The file contains titles, URLs, and a one-sentence AI-generated summary.

**Step 2 - Refine the blurbs**
- I drop the CSV into Copy.ai’s bulk-refine tool. The AI shortens each summary to 30-40 words and adds a friendly hook.
- I quickly scan for any tone mismatches - the AI is good, but it occasionally adds jargon that doesn’t fit my audience.

**Step 3 - Assemble the draft**
- Using a simple Python script (under 20 lines), I read the refined CSV and output a JSON payload that matches MailerLite’s draft schema.
- The script also injects a static header and footer that I reuse every week.

**Step 4 - Schedule and send**
- I run the script, which pushes the draft to MailerLite via its API.
- A quick glance in the dashboard confirms the email looks right, then I hit “Schedule for 4 pm”.

The entire chain runs on my local machine; there’s no need for a cloud server or recurring cron jobs. Once the script is saved, I just double-click it each week.

## Results and what I learned
After three weeks the system showed clear benefits.

- **Time saved:** Roughly two and a half hours per week. I now spend about 30 minutes on the workflow, leaving me with a full two extra hours for client work or personal projects.
- **Revenue added:** I introduced a modest $5 “support” button at the bottom of the newsletter. A handful of readers clicked it, bringing in about $150 a month.
- **Engagement:** Open rates stayed steady in the mid-40s percent range and click-through rates nudged up a bit because the AI-crafted blurbs felt tighter and more actionable.

The biggest surprise was how little maintenance the system required. Feedly AI continues to learn my preferences, so the raw feed stays relevant. Copy.ai occasionally updates its model, but the bulk-refine endpoint remains backward compatible, so the script never breaks.

A concrete example: one week Feedly highlighted an article about a new browser extension I hadn’t seen. The AI summary captured the key benefit in a single sentence, and after I added a short personal note, the link generated the highest click-through of the month. It reminded me that the AI can surface hidden gems you might otherwise miss.

I also learned a few practical lessons:
- **Don’t over-automate the voice.** A single human-written intro still adds personality and keeps the newsletter from feeling like a robot.
- **Keep the tech stack simple.** Adding a fourth tool added complexity without measurable benefit.
- **Test the pricing gently.** The $5 button felt low-key, but it gave readers a clear way to say “thanks” without feeling sold to.

## FAQ
**Q: Do I need any coding experience?**
A: Minimal. The Python script is a copy-paste from a gist I linked in the post. If you can run a .py file, you’re good.

**Q: Can I use a different email service?**
A: Absolutely. MailerLite’s API is straightforward, but most services (ConvertKit, Mailchimp) have similar draft-creation endpoints. You’d just adjust the JSON payload.

**Q: What if Feedly AI stops supporting the export feature?**
A: You can fall back to an RSS-to-CSV converter or even manually copy the highlighted items. The workflow is designed to survive a single tool change.

## Bottom line
Automation doesn’t have to be a massive project. By pairing a smart feed aggregator, a quick-refine AI, and a simple email API, I turned a time-draining newsletter into a 45-minute side hustle that adds $150 a month and frees up two hours of work each week. If you already send a regular newsletter, give this four-step loop a try - the payoff is modest but immediate.
